intro_en: The Israel National Trail continues through a varied landscape of cliffs, dunes, beautiful beaches and an outdoor sculpture park.
character_en: Walking over flat terrain and low dunes. Most of the route is unshaded, but there are shady spots available along it and beaches for refreshing.
transport_en: Bus stops on Road 2 at the entrance to Yakum. Stops near the Yarkon, next to the Reading parking lot.
pois_en: Hof HaSharon National Park. The Arsuf dunes. The Arsuf Kedem sculpture garden. Sidna Ali Beach.
important_en: Entry to Hof HaSharon National Park is free of charge – but the entrance gates may be closed after dark.
Walking on the beach at the foot of Apollonia is forbidden; Apollonia must be bypassed from the east.

There are many water points and options to buy food or sit in restaurants. Near the route's starting point at the entrance to Yakum there are cafes and restaurants that are open on Shabbat too. Further on you can stop at the beach restaurants in Herzliya or at the minimarket next to the Hof HaSharon parking lot.
description_en:
We start the route at the gas station complex at the entrance to Yakum. We head west over a pedestrian bridge above the Coastal Highway, and continue about half a km west.
The trail turns south (on old maps it appears as a blue marking) and reaches a shaded, well-kept seating area. From here the trail skirts Kibbutz Ga'ash and the new neighborhood next to the kibbutz on the west. West of the neighborhood there is a fine lookout over the sea.
Another 100 meters south we reach an unpaved parking lot. Those who wish can "pop" down and back to a wild, unregulated beach. South of the parking lot is the northern entrance gate of Hof HaSharon National Park (a turnstile gate). The trail itself runs along the eastern side of the reserve, but it is highly recommended to leave it for half an hour and turn west with a red-marked trail as far as the cliff above the sea (there is signage too). This is one of the most beautiful stretches along the country's coast. Note: the cliff here is high and there is a danger of collapse in the kurkar (sandstone) cliffs, so do not stray west of the marked trail!
The red marking reaches the southern end of the cliff path and bends east. After a few minutes' walk, at the reserve's southern exit gate, we rejoin the Israel National Trail.
If, on the other hand, we keep walking on the Israel National Trail and do not enter the reserve, we pass through a beautiful stretch of dunes a short distance before the reserve's southern gate.
Outside the southern gate of the reserve there is a good chance of meeting a popular coffee truck.
We continue south to the Arsuf access road and skirt the village on the east (not to be confused with Arsuf Kedem). After the village, it is highly recommended to go back west on an easy path to more fine lookouts above the sea (an extra walk of about 300 meters each way).
The trail passes between small dunes and vegetation – which blooms wonderfully in spring and early summer. About half a km south of Arsuf there is a paragliding "launch pad", which turns into a colorful celebration on weekends.
From the launch-pad area we return east, and a little east of the dirt road we see the small village of Arsuf Kedem. This is an exceptional community in every respect, not officially recognized and whose name does not even appear on maps (see more in the Wikipedia entry). A visit to the nearby "Dina Park" – a special outdoor sculpture park – is recommended.
From the sculpture park we continue for about 1.5 km south parallel to the fence of the old IMI (Israel Military Industries) compound. In spring this is an area rich in blooms.
We proceed to the access road to Apollonia National Park. The trail passes by the entrance to the national park and continues south to the Sidna Ali Mosque. From the parking lot north of the mosque, it is recommended to leave the trail, go down the stairs to the beach and pass by Nissim's "Cave House".
The Israel National Trail itself continues after the mosque along a short internal road (closed by a barrier) leading to a beach. Here there is drinking water, sometimes cold, a lifeguard hut, shade shelters and a wonderful bathing beach.
A few interesting things about the Sidna Ali Mosque: in the mosque compound there is a tomb attributed to the holy warrior Sayyidna Ali (meaning "our master Ali"; Sidna is a shortened form of the word). According to tradition, he was killed in 1250 in a battle against the Crusaders at Apollonia. On Fridays many Muslims come to pray and eat. On the other days of the week it is usually quiet, and you can ask the guard for permission to enter in order to fill up with water and use the toilets.
In the past, the stretch of beach west of the mosque had a beautiful, wide strip of sand. Today only a narrow strip remains, and the cliff is more exposed to the danger of collapse. The culprit is the Herzliya Marina – even though it lies 2 km to the south. How can that be? The marina blocks the passage of most of the sand arriving from the south. This is one of the important reasons for the green organizations' opposition to building more marinas (read more about our campaign against building marinas at the expense of everyone's beaches).
The trail continues along the Herzliya beaches, where you can find water, toilets (next to the elevator), cafes and restaurants. At the end of Acadia Beach we leave the beach for the marina complex – nicknamed "the Monster" by nature and beach lovers.
We continue another 2 km or so south to Tzuk Beach, an official bathing beach with water, toilets and more cafes. We continue to Tel Baruch Beach, walking along a new promenade that the Tel Aviv municipality built between the two beaches. From Tel Baruch Beach the trail continues on a promenade west of the area where Sde Dov Airport used to be.
The promenade reaches a small bridge west of the Reading power station, and at the entrance to the Tel Aviv Port complex, with its abundance of cafes and restaurants, it becomes a wide wooden deck overlooking the sea and the Yarkon estuary.
South of the power station is a tiny ancient mound topped by a concrete pillar. This is Tel Kudadi, and the pillar is a British memorial to the crossing of the Yarkon in World War I – when it was still a rushing river, unlike today, when the flow is from the sea into the river.
For those arriving by car at the end point – a fairly large parking lot, usually with space available, is located about 300 meters from the bridge. Walk along the road adjacent to the power station on its east side, from the parking lot to the bridge and the Yarkon estuary.
Bus stops are located a little to the east, next to the Reading parking lot and Rokach Boulevard.
nearby_en: The Dina Sculpture Park at Arsuf Kedem. The park was established in memory of a local resident who died before her time. The place is beautiful all year round, and especially with the spring bloom. The sculpture park begins north of the small village and continues to its west and south (not to be confused with Arsuf).
The Arsuf dunes – see in the route description the section passing through the area south of Arsuf and west of the Israel National Trail.

Ga'ash Beach – the way down to it is along a jeep track from the northern parking lot of Hof HaSharon National Park. The beach has no toilets, water or lifeguard, and bathing is not recommended because of the rocks. But it has shallow lagoons suitable for children. In certain sections, a little removed from the beach access point, some people bathe dressed as Adam and Eve...
author_en: Omer Shapira, content coordinator, Tourism Department, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
